When presenting such a tool, it should be a must to include a live demo, i.e. a link to a fully-featured set-up of the app so that readers can get a feel for it before deciding when they want to use it. I couldn't find any such link, neither in the paper nor in the repository. This should be amended.

Similarly, it would be good to provide users trying to set up the app an example dataset that's appropriately prepared (could be the same as the one used in the example above, or a subset thereof).

At the moment, installation is a pain. The package depends on lots of packages that are neither in cran nor in bioconductor, and one has to figure out where they are. Specifically, rbokeh, ggvolc and scToppR need to be installed manually. When going to the scToppR github page, the installation command doesn't work because scToppR is not in bioconductor. Similarly, the package depends on rbokeh, whose main information in the repository is that it is not actively maintained.

In the end I had to do this to install:

```

BiocManager::install(c("BioinformaticsMUSC/scToppR", "bokeh/rbokeh", "loukesio/ggvolc", "BioinformaticsMUSC/ShinyCellPlus"))

```

Users abandon early, and this lack of user-friendliness already at the installation stage makes one wary of the rest of the package: the feeling it gives is that the authors haven't really asked external users to try it.

It would be important to include some idea of the scalability. I appreciate the way the dataset is prepared and stored as h5 to ease memory requirements, this seems nicely done. Are the plots simply vector ggplots, which would become unmanageable with large datasets, or do they implement some rasterization or are they based on something more scalable? It's not a tragedy if the package is only applicable to small/medium-sized datasets, but users need to know before trying it.

The dataset and app preparation happens smoothly from a user perspective. At the same time, it seems like this could be achieved from other formats as well, e.g. an AnnData object. In general, it feels like many of the extra functionalities added in ShinyCellPlus are dependent on specific ways of doing the analysis (e.g. doing GO enrichment using ToppGene). This isn't optimal, but passable, I guess.

A key question I was left with is how this compares with other available tools, in particular iSEE. What was the rationale for a new tool? Are there things that ShinyCellPlus can do, and which iSEE can't? or, since this seems unlikely given iSEE's flexibility and custom plugins, are there things that are much simpler to do? This might be worth some discussion.

MINOR COMMENTS:

- There are a lot of little things in the functions that make user experience unnecessarily complicated. For example, I needed to specify the assay (which isn't done in the docs, presumably because the assay is named something recognized), but the error message wasn't very instructive. One could either fetch the default assay (and mention this) or at least outputs a useful error message saying that this was specified. Similarly, if scConf is left null, it could simply be computed on the fly to use defaults.

- The documentation says, "The Shiny App should run upon completion of this script", but it doesn't: the script simply creates a shinyApp folder, in which one has to go and manually launch the app.

- As one interacts with the app, the console reports many errors, and while these do not impair the usage of the app, it does suggest that the inputs to reactive functions are not appropriately checked, and this litters the logs with unnecessary warnings that can make debugging more difficult.

- The readme discusses the fact that it can take some time for the app to load. The authors could consider a splash page showing that something is happening (and at the same time allowing for some name/icon of the dataset/instance to appear), which can be easily implemented for instance with the waiter package.

- It might be useful to split the documentation, for example a user trying to test the app for the first time doesn't necessarily need to read through the whole Libra part...

By and large the paper has adequate scope, in my reviewers report, I will concentrate on the areas of improvement.

The 
                introduction part can be enriched further, after stating the objective of the papers, the authors, need to provide further justification on why the objectives are important why should we care about the study objectives. Secondly, the authors need to mention their unique contribution in this area of study. Lastly, towards the end of the introduction sections, it’s good to give us a glimpse of the paper organization, sections in the paper, methods, data and variables. So that by the time we are done reading introduction part we are able to grasp whole picture of the study.

Literature review

It seems the literature review has been divided into two parts 
                The
                
                National Innovation System (NIS), and 
                Science, Technology, and Innovation Policies (STIP) in Emerging Economies

My observation is that the literature on NIS is very brief mainly focusing on the importance of NIS. I advise the authors to look at the composition of NIS.  The current literature is at quintuple helix (recent works of EG Carayannis). I expect the authors discuss how the five helix are interconnected in Ethiopia.  Secondly, the authors need to mention on the measurement of NIS productivity by discussing the inputs and outputs of NIS (literature by Global innovation index GII). Lastly Factors hindering effective functioning of NIS, ought to be mentioned here in general.

On the Science, Technology, and Innovation Policies (STIP) in Emerging Economies part

I expected the authors to discuss here regional and local  policies like ASTII ,  STISA 2014-24 and Agenda 2063, and describe how Ethiopia is catching and implementing this policies . I also expected to hear about Ethiopia STI policy implementation framework. Is there a commission STI, a national innovation agony or even a national research fund in Ethiopia?

Methods

I suggest a table showing the four categories of the documents received, and the objectives would have been clearer. The readers may want know which documents were reviewed per study objective.

Ethiopia, Kenya, and Rwanda Experience

I did not see any justification provided for comparing innovation in these three countries given the fact that they don’t belong to the income level!! . I advise the authors to compare economic peers or all countries in eastern Africa region including others like Uganda Tanzania Sudan etc. the authors can also compare Ethiopia with other lower income countries in sub-Saharan Africa.

Secondly, I advise the authors to use graphs to compare the countries, visual graphics,/maps are very effective in countries comparison.

Findings/in terms of opportunities and challenges

These finding I suggest they be presented in form of a table for clarity and focus – each opportunity or challenge be accompanied by the document reviewed.

The article requires substantial revisions to strengthen its overall structure, clarity, and coherence. These improvements are crucial for the manuscript to meet the indexing standards and increase its potential for successful acceptance. Specifically, the following areas need significant attention:

1. 
                Conceptual Clarification:

The focus of the paper should be clearly defined—whether it addresses regional innovation systems (RIS) or national innovation systems (NIS). The current overlap between these two perspectives creates conceptual ambiguity. Adding a section that explains the distinctions and linkages between the two systems is highly recommended.

Alternatively, if the focus is on the national level, the title and literature should reflect that appropriately.

To enhance the coherence and academic rigor of the study, I recommend the following adjustments:

1. Add a dedicated section that defines and differentiates the concepts of Regional Innovation Systems (RIS) and National Innovation Systems (NIS). This section should explain the distinct features, theoretical frameworks, and interconnections between these two systems.

2. Clarify how the regional perspective relates to the national system in Ethiopia, and explicitly state whether the focus is on regional innovation within the broader national framework or purely national-level innovation policies.

3. Alternatively, if the primary focus is on the national system, the title and literature should be adjusted to reflect that. The author should replace the current references with relevant literature on national innovation systems and national development strategies.

4. If the intention is to maintain the focus on the regional level, the analysis should shift to regional innovation dynamics and regional development frameworks, ensuring alignment with the core concept of Regional Innovation Systems.

2. Methodological Enhancement:

Incorporating a SWOT-TOWS analysis, as outlined in the article Samara, E., Kilintzis, P., Grammenou, A. 
                et al. Towards Transformative Innovation Policy in Territorial Governance: Mapping the Relevance of RRI Elements. 
                J Knowledge Economy (2024 [Ref-1]). 
                https://doi.org/10.1007/s13132-024-02320-1, would provide a more structured and practical framework for developing improvement strategies. This methodology will help ensure that the recommendations are specific, actionable, and policy-oriented. Presenting the proposed strategies in a comprehensive table will also enhance the clarity and accessibility of the findings.

By incorporating TOWS analysis, the author could:

1. Align internal strengths with external opportunities to propose proactive strategies.

2. Mitigate internal weaknesses by leveraging external opportunities or reducing threats.

3. Ensure a policy-focused approach with clear, tangible outputs that are relevant to stakeholders and decision-makers.

3. Policy Strategy Integration:

The suggested strategies should be consolidated into a coherent section or table that highlights key priorities and links them to the identified challenges and opportunities. This will create a stronger, policy-relevant narrative that aligns with international best practices in innovation system analysis.

These revisions will significantly improve the article’s impact, making it more relevant for both academic and policy audiences. Careful attention to these recommendations will enhance the paper’s conceptual consistency, methodological rigor, and practical relevance, ensuring its readiness for indexing.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

From a strong literature review, the paper proposes an integration of key concepts in Higher Education learning and academic achievement: intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, critical thinking, and self-regulation. The aim here is to empirically establish how these relate between themselves, looking at how they predict academic achievement. With a fairly decent sample of HE students in Greece and through solid statistical methods, the researchers achieve their purposes in arguing for a pathway model. The research is strong and highly valuable for the field, clearly stemming from an Educational Psychology background.

Still, from a Higher Education Research perspective, this paper could be better understood if taken in relation with this latter field. It would be fair to assume that culturally and historically Higher Education has been a privilege and luxury for society for a long time, and only recently it has been transformed by its massification and democratization, and most current by its neo liberalization and marketisation. What once was considered to be a voluntary endeavour for the privileged and capable, some would argue that now it has been increasingly believed to be a necessity (regardless of the personal/developmental or systemic/economic reasoning behind it).

To some degree, the question this paper asks implies that students are not necessarily motivated or engaged in HE beforehand, that they may not be critical thinkers, nor that they believe to be capable, and thus constitutes a new space for academic research. Here I do not argue with these ideas, nor I challenge them; instead, I want to offer an alternative route for arguing for the value and rationale for this paper. As I see it, looking at this from the field of Educational Psychology the issue is not new per se; in contrast, it very well may be so for Higher Education Research. Of course, setting up a further and larger context would most likely change this paper substantially as much as it would support its claim. My suggestion is not to rework it but to properly extend it into the field of Higher Education as a further development for future research. I see the paper as perfectly consistent as it is, working itself from Ed Psych.

I will elaborate on a few aspects of the paper that have not been already addressed in past reviews.

In a general sense, the literature review does what it promises, it offers a vast and well-balanced look at the field. Still, I see two main point for further development, one internal and one external. Internally, the section would benefit from an editorial review, as it is easy to find more than a few very broad and bold statements about how the concepts relate to each other without necessarily being supported by the argumentation threads. Moreover, proofreading could be useful as (a) some sentences could be refined and (b) the text could get a more cohesive feel. Externally, I wonder if a literature review is the only section needed prior to the aim and research hypotheses section. It seems that the paper is trying to establish relationships that are not clearly taken from the literature. As the section does not refer explicitly to how the conceptual relationships are established (for example, how they are not correlational), I see that a theoretical/conceptual section could be useful. Using theory to argue for conceptual relationships could offer an avenue that empirical findings on their own do not.

(In future projects) I would encourage the research team to  explore turning the paper on its head and start from a conceptual critique of the field and how each concept should/could relate to each other to make sense of the general learning process, for then contrasting such vision with empirical research.

As an example of such work, I would suggest a critical review of the (intrinsic/extrinsic) motivation conceptualization. I'd question the internal consistency of such dichotomy and its value for understanding the issue. It seems that intrinsic motivation does not necessarily 'originate from within' the learner as said. In the literature review section, the argument for intrinsic motivation being influenced by a series of factors and so internalized could very well be read as it being developed or learnt. In that sense, internalization could be read from a Vygotskian perspective and so the distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic could be turned from an essential to developmental. So, the idea of an intrinsic motivation can be transformed as a more stably internalized motivation. This line of reasoning could open up the idea of a developing motivation for learning.

This paper instead leaves the theoretical developments as hanging from empirical research without articulating internally how this may be. On the theoretical implications section, the team states that "that educational theories must consider the dynamic and reciprocal relationships between motivation, cognitive processes, and self-regulation to fully capture the complexities of academic achievement.". Still, the whole paper has been about unidirectional relationships by arguing for a path model. This is problematic because this statement reads as trying to situate itself within a holistic approach that it is in fact not taking. The conceptual relationships that have been developed here have been supported mainly by the method which sets the data into a particular order for then proving if that work. Here, the main accomplishment is that it works, but the downside is that it has been clearly underdeveloped theoretically.

Lastly, regarding the future directions, the first paragraph seems moderately justified, yet it could use some improvement; moreover, the second paragraph reads more capricious and slightly outdated (for example, touching on learning styles which have been largely debunked).

Overall, this paper is definitely valuable. Here, my suggestions are either cosmetic or future-oriented. Cosmetically, I suggest that the paper is reviewed to simplify and clean up its contribution. It is doing enough, yet that needs to be stated humbly and realistically. In a future oriented manner, I suggest to (i) contextualize the value of these concepts and line of research looking directly at the Higher Education research field, and (ii) theoretically address the concepts to internally articulate them, and then evaluate the benefits and hindrances of any empirical research model like the pathway one.

This study offers a relevant and well-executed analysis of how managerial ability affects working capital management efficiency (WCME) in large Indian firms. The authors use Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) to measure efficiency (managerial ability - MA) and Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) for regression modeling. These approaches are methodologically appropriate. However, several important revisions are needed to meet the publication standards.

The theoretical framework is currently too broad and should be narrowed to focus on one or two main theories, such as UET and RBV, to improve coherence. Moreover, the writing should be more concise and avoid vague or technical language that could confuse readers. Updating references with more recent studies from top-tier journals would also strengthen the paper’s relevance and credibility.

The most serious issue is the lack of control for endogeneity, which raises doubts about whether managerial ability truly causes improvements in WCME.

First, DEA assumes a deterministic production frontier, ignoring measurement error and noise. This is problematic, especially when applied to a decade of financial data across heterogeneous firms. The lack of sensitivity analysis or alternative models like Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) limits confidence in the efficiency estimates. Second, while GEE accounts for within-panel correlation, it fails to address endogeneity. The link between MA and WCME is likely bi-directional, whereby better WCME may attract capable managers, and vice versa. GEE offers population-averaged estimates, not causal inference, unless strict assumptions are met. No IVs, lagged variables, or dynamic panel methods (e.g., System GMM) are employed to mitigate this. Third, MA is measured using a two-step DEA and regression approach per Demerjian et al. (2012), but the paper omits key details about the first-stage regression. This raises doubts about whether firm-level heterogeneity was properly controlled.

Last but not least, the manuscript would benefit from clearer visual representations of the results, such as charts showing how the impact of managerial ability changes across different firm types.

This article explores the integration of mobile payments into the realm of research, with the objective of elucidating the technological, socio-economic, and cultural factors that influence user experience and satisfaction, thereby attracting a greater number of users. A systematic literature review based on the PRISMA 2020 framework was conducted to select 63 documents from Scopus and WoS. This review explored research trends in mobile payment adoption. The most frequently utilized models for this analysis are the extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the extended Unified Theory of Acceptance of Technology (UTAUT). The most salient variables in this study are social influence, perceived security, perceived risk, trust, and perceived benefits. Consequently, it is recommended that future research agendas prioritize subjects such as biometric authentication, payment flexibility, and contactless payments. From a business perspective, there is an emphasis on the development of more intuitive user interfaces.

This article provides a valuable roadmap for future research, particularly in identifying underexplored variables. The topic of this research is highly relevant and timely, particularly in light of the rapid advancements in digital finance and payment systems. The article is well-structured and clearly presented, contributing to its overall readability and coherence. The methodology employed is appropriate and provides meaningful insights for both theoretical development and practical application in the field.

Nevertheless, with minor revisions,  there are several areas that require further clarification and refinement in order to enhance the clarity, accuracy, and academic rigor of the paper. Below are some key points identified in the article that could benefit from improvement:

1) Inclusion of Database Search Timeframe

The article does not specify the timeframe during which the database searches were conducted in Scopus and Web of Science (WoS). This information is crucial, as the number of publications indexed in these databases evolves continuously, potentially influencing the comprehensiveness and accuracy of the literature analysis. To ensure consistency and reproducibility, it is recommended that future studies clearly report the exact dates of database searches and conduct them simultaneously in both Scopus and WoS to minimize discrepancies and maintain methodological rigor.

2) Inclusion of References as Scientific Evidence

Several statements presented in the introduction section appear to reflect opinions or conclusions that are not supported by appropriate scholarly references. It is strongly recommended to ensure that all such assertions be accompanied by relevant citations from credible academic sources. Incorporating references will strengthen the validity and credibility of the claims made, grounding them in existing scientific literature and enhancing the overall academic rigor of the paper.

3) Clarity Regarding the Use of Analytical Tools

This article does mention the use of Microsoft Excel and VOSViewer; however, the nature of the analysis and the specific analytical methods used remain unclear. For example, in Figure 7, what analytical approach was used, and what tools were utilized? Furthermore, Figure 8 suggests that the visualization is the result of burst analysis using the Scitespace tool. This statement is speculative, as the source material does not explicitly address this point. Clear explanations and elaborations are essential. To enhance methodological transparency and reproducibility, this study should provide a clear mapping between the tools used and the specific analyses conducted.

4) Clarify the PRISMA Flow Diagram

The stages in the PRISMA method have already been explained in the section on inclusion and exclusion criteria. However, it is still unclear to me what the criteria are for “report not retrievable = 305” and also for “record excluded = 167.” It would be better to present the criteria in the PRISMA flow diagram.

5) Discussion on Limited Practical Case Studies

The number of practical case studies employed to illustrate theoretical insights is limited. It is imperative to provide concrete examples of successful mobile payment systems in diverse contexts.
